\begin{center}
{\large\bfseries Naive Diversification and the Opportunity Set:\\[2pt]
Long-Only Equity Factor Indices}\\[16pt]
\quita{August 2026} \nuevo{October 2026}

\vspace{12pt}
\section*{ABSTRACT}

\begin{quitado}
For twenty years the argument over whether portfolio optimization beats equal weighting has
gone unresolved. We show that both sides are right on their own data. What divides them is the
menu of assets on offer.

On the menu a real equity investor can reach, twenty-eight long-only regional factor indices,
no optimization rule beats equal weighting by a margin this much data can settle. We race
seventeen rules over 210 months out of sample, testing every comparison for significance. The
optimizers are not at fault: these indices are close to being the same bet. Long-only factor
tilts within a region move almost in lockstep, so the whole menu carries barely more
independent risk than one index, and no weighting scheme can manufacture diversification the
menu does not contain. Three asset classes, Treasuries, gold and cash, add more of it than all
twenty-eight equity indices combined.

For a retail investor, widening the menu is the only move with measurable evidence behind it.
\end{quitado}

\begin{nuevotexto}
Does portfolio optimization beat simply splitting money equally? Twenty years of research
disagree. We test seventeen rules on the menu a retail investor can actually buy, twenty-eight
long-only regional factor indices, under five performance measures, with fund fees, and on
training windows reaching back to 2002. No rule beats equal weighting by a margin the data can
settle, and after allowing for the number of rules tried none loses by such a margin either. The
leader, minimum variance, shows no detectable return beyond its exposures to profitable and
low-risk stocks. The indices are nearly one bet, yet that redundancy is not the explanation we
expected: across twelve menus, the rules' edge does not grow with diversification. Changing the
menu itself does more. Adding Treasuries and gold cuts drawdowns sharply and, over 54 years,
raises the Sharpe ratio significantly, though 17 years of data cannot settle that gain.
\end{nuevotexto}
\nota{ATENCI\'ON: cambia la tesis. La auditor\'ia del 30-10 (M57) prob\'o en 12 men\'us que la dispersi\'on NO decide si optimizar funciona, y (M58) que ``tres activos a\~naden m\'as que los 28 \'indices'' era aritm\'eticamente falso. El t\'itulo ``...and the Opportunity Set'' quiz\'a ya no encaje; decide t\'u. Resumen: 157 palabras.}

\section*{KEY TAKEAWAYS}

\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item \quita{On the menu a retail investor can reach, no weighting rule beats equal weight by a margin
      this data can resolve. The test carries 56\% power, so an edge the size of the largest
      one observed would have gone undetected about half the time.}
      \nuevo{On the menu a retail investor can reach, no weighting rule beats equal weight by a
      margin the data can resolve, by Sharpe, Sortino, Treynor or information ratio, with or
      without the 2008 crisis. A true gain of 0.20 in Sharpe ratio would be detected only about
      half the time, so this is ``not shown'', not ``none''.}
\item \quita{The binding constraint is the menu, not the optimizer. Twenty-eight long-only
      \emph{equity} factor indices hold 1.31 independent risk bets, and adding Treasuries,
      gold and cash buys more than all of them.}
      \nuevo{The leader, minimum variance, earns its edge from known exposures: no alpha is
      detectable once profitability and low beta are priced. Twenty-eight equity indices hold 1.31
      independent bets, but on menus twice as diversified the rules gain no more.}
\item \quita{Widen the menu before refining the weights. Optimization pays where holdings
      genuinely differ, and an investable equity factor menu offers very little difference
      to exploit.}\nuevo{A world index plus Treasuries, gold and cash holds 2.78 bets against 1.31.
      That cuts risk at once; a better risk-adjusted return shows only over decades.}
\end{itemize}

\vspace{12pt}
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} naive diversification; 1/N; factor investing; equity
indices; portfolio choice; diversification ratio; backtest overfitting.

%  MAIN TEXT — begins on the third page.
%  PMR: "Articles in PMR publications do not include any heading before
%  an article's introductory material." The introduction therefore carries

%  Section 2 — which is what the prose cross-references point at. Nothing
%  in the text refers to "Section 1".

Whether portfolio optimization beats naive equal weight is one of the
longest-running unresolved questions in asset allocation, and the disagreement
is unusually sharp. \citet{demiguel2009} found that across fourteen models and
seven datasets nothing consistently beats 1/N\nuevo{ (equal weighting: the same share of capital in each of the $N$ assets)} out of sample\nuevo{ (on data the rule did not see when it chose its weights)}, and the most recent
replication, on the original datasets extended twenty years through the global
financial crisis and the pandemic, reaches the same verdict
\citep{gelmini2024}. An equally serious literature holds that the result is an
artifact. On that account 1/N wins only because the optimizers were fed
short-window sample means \citep{kritzman2010}, or because they were tested in
high-turnover forms that transaction costs destroy \citep{kirby2012}. Both sides
show real out-of-sample evidence. The debate has stayed open because it has been
argued as though it had a single answer.

\quita{It does not, and this article locates the answer.} \nuevo{A natural conjecture is that the
answer depends on the setting.} Whether optimization beats 1/N
turns on five things: the dispersion of the asset menu, the length and quality of
the estimation inputs, how much turnover the strategy generates, whether short
sales and leverage are permitted, and how demanding a bar ``beat'' must clear.
Fix all five at the position a real retail investor occupies, a \emph{long-only, index-based, factor-tilted equity menu} with realistic data length, transaction
costs charged and statistical significance required, and the question has a clean answer. On that menu no weighting rule beats 1/N at
conventional significance, and Section 5.1 reports the power behind that statement. \quita{The cause is a property of the menu
itself, which holds about one independent bet, leaving no dispersion for any
scheme to exploit. The optimization defenders are right on their datasets, where
dispersion is high. We are right on ours, where it is not. The two findings are
compatible once the opportunity set is named. Section 6 measures it
(Exhibits~\ref{ex:frontier} and~\ref{ex:dispersion}).} \nuevo{The statement holds under five
performance measures, with fund fees, and on training windows that bring the 2002 and 2008 bear
markets into the race (Sections 5.3 and 5.4). We then test the obvious explanation, that this menu
is too redundant for any rule to exploit, by running the same rules on eleven other menus. The
explanation fails: the rules' edge does not grow with diversification (Section 6.2).}

We field the canonical construction rules together with the three most-cited rules built
specifically to beat 1/N, race them under one protocol, and report a $p$-value for every
ranking claim. We make three contributions.

\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{6pt}
\item \quita{\textbf{The reconciling finding.} We measure why
1/N is unbeatable on an investable factor menu. The diversification ratio implies
1.31 independent bets (95\% confidence interval 1.24 to 1.40 by circular block
bootstrap), long-only factor tilts co-move at 0.885, and the covariance is
near-singular. The mechanism is confirmed by contrast: adding three asset classes
raises the ratio to 1.43, a paired difference of $+0.120$ at $p = 0.0002$, and
moves the menu's minimum pairwise correlation from 0.53 to $-0.14$. This places
the twenty-year 1/N debate on a single axis, the opportunity set.}
\nuevo{\textbf{A test of the menu explanation.} The diversification ratio, which measures how much
of the assets' individual risk cancels out when held together, implies 1.31 independent bets on
this menu (95\% confidence interval 1.24 to 1.40, from a bootstrap that rebuilds thousands of
alternative histories from blocks of consecutive months). The tempting conclusion is that
redundancy is why nothing beats 1/N. We test it across twelve menus and it fails: from 1999 the
minimum-variance edge is largest on the most redundant menus (rank correlation $-0.69$), and since
1963 it is close to zero on all of them. Changing the menu does change the outcome: a world index
plus Treasuries, gold and cash holds 2.78 bets, and such menus raise the Sharpe ratio significantly
over 54 years, though not yet over 17.}

\item \textbf{Inference on every comparison.} We run the following as
standing diagnostics on every build: \citet{ledoit2008} bootstrap Sharpe
inference (the robust successor to the Jobson-Korkie test of \citeyear{jobson1981} that the prior replication uses), deflated Sharpe ratios \citep{bailey2014}\nuevo{, which discount the best result for
the number of strategies tried}, a Friedman-Nemenyi joint test
\citep{demsar2006}, the combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV) probability of backtest overfitting \citep{bailey2017}, leave-one-region-out re-races, and sensitivity grids over costs, refit cadence,
constraints, block length and the covariance estimator. Under it, all three
published ``beat-1/N'' rules we field fail. \citeauthor{yuan2023}'s
\citeyearpar{yuan2023} combination loses outright, \citeauthor{brodie2009}'s
\citeyearpar{brodie2009} sparse portfolio reaches only \quita{$p = 0.149$} \nuevo{$p = 0.193$}, and HERC
lands below both its parents.\nuevo{ This version adds Sortino, Treynor, information and
appraisal ratios and CAPM and multifactor alphas against global factors, each tested against
1/N with a family-wise correction for the number of rules tried, an illustrative charge for fund
fees, and re-races on shorter and rolling training windows whose scored period includes the 2002 and
2008 bear markets.}

\item \textbf{A pre-registered estimator that does not work.} We build, freeze and
pre-register a regime-conditioned shrinkage estimator\nuevo{, a rule that pulls noisy
per-regime average returns toward a longer-history estimate,} then attack it, and the
macro regime signal it depends on, with placebo tests on the regime layer\nuevo{ (re-running
everything with the regime labels deliberately scrambled)}. Both return nothing resolvable at this sample size. We report the
negative result with a power post-mortem.
\end{enumerate}

Section 2 sets out the five conditions the disagreement turns on, and Section 3 fixes them at
the position a retail investor occupies, on a menu of twenty-eight index sleeves. Section 4
gives the protocol and the inference every ranking claim has to clear. Section 5 reports what
the comparison can and cannot detect\nuevo{, including measures beyond the Sharpe ratio and a
window that contains the 2008 crisis}; Section 6, \quita{the contribution, measures the menu itself and
explains why Section 5 comes out as it does.}\nuevo{measures the menu and tests whether its redundancy explains Section 5.} Sections 7 to 9 extend the menu, test the regime
layer, and set out the robustness checks and the limitations.\nuevo{ Appendix A defines every
contestant in plain terms; Appendix B reports the factor data, the factor loadings and the
net-of-fees results.}

\setcounter{section}{1}
\section{The debate and its five levers}

The two sides rarely engage on the same terms. On one side, \citet{demiguel2009}
and, most recently, \citet{gelmini2024} find 1/N is not systematically beaten out
of sample. On the other, \citet{kritzman2010}, titling their rebuttal ``the
fallacy of 1/N,'' and \citet{kirby2012} show optimization can win. Read together,
their disagreement concerns experimental conditions, and it resolves into five
levers. (i) \emph{Menu dispersion}: DeMiguel's own explanation, quoted approvingly
by Gelmini and Uberti, is that optimization improves relative to 1/N when
idiosyncratic volatility is high and the covariance is far from singular\nuevo{, that is,
when the assets carry much risk of their own and do not all move together}.
(ii) \emph{Estimation inputs}: Kritzman et al.\ locate 1/N's edge in short-window
sample means. Gelmini and Uberti test the lever directly and find a growing window
helps the optimizers without producing a systematic win. (iii) \emph{Turnover}:
Kirby and Ostdiek attribute the result to the extreme turnover of the strategies
DeMiguel tested. (iv) \emph{Short sales and leverage}: much of the measured
optimization advantage requires positions a long-only investor cannot take.
(v) \emph{The significance bar}: pro-optimization evidence is often point-estimate
or single-dataset, whereas the 1/N side demands significance across datasets.
\citet{pflug2012} supply the theory that side otherwise lacks, showing 1/N
optimal under sufficient model ambiguity, which is the regime a retail investor
with a few decades of data inhabits. We fix all five levers at that retail
position.

\head{Estimation error.} \citet{markowitz1952} optimality collides with sampling
error \citep{michaud1989,chopra1993}, which \citet{demiguel2009} quantify.
\citet{yuan2023} supply the missing theory. The Sharpe ratio an investor actually realizes from estimated weights converges to
$\tau \cdot SR$, a fraction $\tau$ of the true Sharpe ratio $SR$, where
$\tau = \sqrt{(1-\eta)/(1+\eta/SR^{2})}$ and $\eta = N/T$ is the number of assets per
observation. The more assets a menu carries per month of data, the more of the attainable
Sharpe ratio estimation destroys.\nuevo{ In words: with many assets and few months of data, a
rule that has to estimate its inputs keeps only part of the performance it would earn with
perfect knowledge.} Under a one-factor structure\nuevo{ (one common driver, such as the equity
market, explaining most of the movement)} 1/N is asymptotically
optimal as $N$ grows. They
then beat 1/N with a closed-form combination of the plug-in global
minimum-variance portfolio and 1/N. We field their rule (Section 5), where it
loses on our menu, an outcome their own Proposition 3 and their $T = 360$ window
requirement predict in advance. The 1/N result therefore survives its
strongest published challenger, adjudicated with that challenger's mathematics.
\nota{cr\'itica posible: en \texttt{rules.py} la $\lambda^{*}$ de Yuan-Zhou est\'a RE-DERIVADA, no transcrita de su ec. (29). Hay que cotejarla con el art\'iculo publicado antes de sostener esta frase.}

\head{Menu selection.} A weighting study is only as interesting as its menu.
\citet{ilmanen2012} report average correlation near zero across \emph{factor}
constituents against roughly 0.4 across asset classes, which is why a
factor-spanning menu should diversify more per slot. We measure our own menu with
the metric that literature standardized, the \citet{choueifaty2008}
diversification ratio, whose square estimates the number of independent risk bets.
Section 6 shows that the long-only wrapper destroys most of the effect.
\citet{hurst2017} point at a diversifier we do not hold. We field the rule form of
trend here and flag the asset form as the more promising route.

\head{Structural weighting rules.} Risk parity and equal risk contribution
\citep{maillard2010,asness2012}\nuevo{, which give every asset the same share of total risk
rather than of capital}, hierarchical risk parity \citep{lopezdeprado2016}\nuevo{, which groups
similar assets into a tree and splits capital down it,}
and minimum variance \citep{clarke2006}\nuevo{, the least volatile combination available}, whose success the low-volatility anomaly
explains \citep{haugen1991,frazzini2014}, win by imposing structure instead of
estimating means. \citet{antonov2025} supply the theory hierarchical risk parity
lacked, showing analytically that its weights carry less estimation-induced noise
than plug-in Markowitz's. \citet{raffinot2018} hybridizes the two families as
HERC, with a gap-index cluster count after \citet{tibshirani2001}. We field both
linkages, since reporting only the flattering one is how hyperparameters get
hidden.

\head{Constraints, sparsity and shrinkage.} \citet{jagannathan2003} showed weight
constraints act as covariance shrinkage, and we measure the effect prospectively
in Section 5.2. \citet{brodie2009} regularize Markowitz with an $\ell_1$ penalty\nuevo{ (a charge on the sum
of absolute weights, which pushes small positions to zero)}
and outperform 1/N on 48 industry portfolios, but that penalty is inert without
shorting (Section 4.2), which makes them the selecting sibling of our spreading
constraints and the natural contestant to field with the two things their claim
lacked, a Sharpe-difference test and transaction costs.
\citet{demiguel2009norm} are the norm-constrained cousin. On the input side,
\citet{jorion1986} and \citet{frost1986} shrink means\nuevo{ (pull noisy estimates toward a
steadier target)} toward within-sample grand
means, whereas ours (Section 4.1) shrinks conditional means toward another era's
evidence under a pretest gate in the \citet{judge1978} lineage.
\citet{boyd2024} show what Markowitz looks like when the inputs are genuinely
there, which is the opposite of the regime we study.

\head{Regime models and inference.} \citet{ang2002,ang2004} established that
regimes matter for allocation, and \citet{guidolin2007} extended the latent-state
machinery\nuevo{, models in which the economy switches between unobserved states}. We differ in kind, using an observable deterministic classifier and
pooled sample means, with nothing fitted to predict. For inference we implement,
in code, \citet{ledoit2008}, \citet{bailey2014}, \citet{bailey2017},
\citet{demsar2006} and \citet{politis1994}. \citeauthor{ledoit2020}'s
\citeyearpar{ledoit2020} analytical nonlinear shrinkage enters as a sensitivity
dimension on the covariance estimator every risk number rides on.

\begin{nuevotexto}
\head{Performance measurement.} The Sharpe ratio charges every unit of volatility equally.
\citet{sortino1991} charge only downside volatility, which matters when strategies differ in how
lopsided their returns are, and \citet{treynor1965} charges only market beta, the risk that
cannot be diversified away inside a larger portfolio. The information ratio
\citep{goodwin1998,grinold2000} measures a strategy against a benchmark, here 1/N, by the
steadiness of its outperformance. \citet{jensen1968} alpha asks a sharper question, whether any
return is left once a strategy's exposures to common risk factors are paid for, and the
appraisal ratio of \citet{treynor1973} scales that alpha by the risk the factors leave
unexplained. The factors are size and value \citep{fama1993}, momentum \citep{carhart1997}, and
profitability and investment \citep{fama2015}, the international versions for an international
menu \citep{fama2012,fama2017}. Profitability is the academic factor closest to the Quality
sleeves \citep{novymarx2013,asness2019}. Standard errors follow \citet{newey1987}.
\end{nuevotexto}

\section{Data and the investor's constraint set}

The menu is not an arbitrary choice of dataset. It is a \emph{position}, and the
article's question only means something once that position is stated. We study a
retail investor who is \emph{long-only, unlevered, index-based and long-horizon}, the constraint set of someone buying liquid, low-cost ETFs rather
than running a book. We price the equity-heavy stance without recommending it.
Our scenario cones put an equity profile's probability of cumulative loss at
approximately \quita{14\%} \nuevo{11\%} at 5 years against a defensive multi-asset profile's \quita{1.4\%} \nuevo{0.9\%},
but at 20 years the two are \quita{1.2\%} \nuevo{1.1\%} and 0.0\% with the equity profile's median
compound annual growth rate still materially higher (approximately \quita{9.7\% versus
7.3\%} \nuevo{9.8\% versus 6.4\%}). Converging \emph{loss probability} is not converging \emph{risk}, since
terminal-wealth dispersion grows with horizon, and these are simulations under a
re-sequenced-history assumption, not forecasts.

The factor tilts are justified by documented return premia and not by
diversification: value and size \citep{fama1993}, momentum \citep{jegadeesh1993}
and quality \citep{asness2019}, with \citet{asness2013} supplying the strongest
anti-data-mining defence. We call each index line, one per region and factor, a sleeve; a region's Reference sleeve is its plain market index, carrying no factor tilt. On our own sleeves every
factor beats its regional Reference in compound annual growth over the full window (Enhanced Value
$+3.70$pt, Momentum $+2.88$pt, Quality $+1.47$pt, winning in 7 of 7, 7 of 7 and
6 of 6 regions). Restricted to the backfill-free live-index era (2015 onward) the premia shrink but survive, with
Momentum $+3.38$pt, Enhanced Value $+1.76$pt and Quality $+1.04$pt, the last
winning in only 4 of 6 regions. That attenuation is consistent with
\citeauthor{mclean2016}'s \citeyearpar{mclean2016} post-publication decay, and it
is the magnitude a prospective investor should plan around. Section 6 measures
that in long-only form these tilts do not diversify.

\head{Sources.} The modern menu is 28 MSCI region-by-factor indices (ACWI, World,
World ex-USA, USA, EM, Europe, AC Asia ex-Japan, Japan, crossed with Reference, Momentum, Enhanced Value and Quality), monthly net-USD total returns,
common window January 1999 to June 2026 (330 months). Four of the 32 possible combinations have
no index, which is why the menu is 28 rather than 32: Europe has no Quality sleeve, World none
for Enhanced Value, and World ex-USA neither Momentum nor Quality. The menu is redundant by
construction, with a mean pairwise correlation of 0.76 and a first principal component
explaining 77\% of variance\nuevo{ (a single common movement accounts for three quarters of
all the month-to-month variation)}.

Two summaries of that redundancy recur below and answer different questions, so we distinguish
them once here. The eigenvalue-entropy effective bet count (approximately 2.8) measures how
many components the variance is spread over\nuevo{, that is, how evenly the menu's movement is
shared among independent directions}. The Choueifaty-Coignard $DR^{2}$ (1.31, Section 6)
measures how much of the sleeves' standalone risk the correlations actually cancel under the
weights held. A menu can spread variance over several components while cancelling almost none
of it, which is exactly this menu. All headline statements use $DR^{2}$.

Sixteen FRED indicators feed a four-quadrant growth-by-inflation classifier, used
for descriptive statistics only with no fitted latent-state model. For long
history we use Ken French research factors (1926 onward) and six long-only
size-by-value portfolios, 10-year US Treasury total returns constructed from the
FRED yield by the \citet{swinkels2019} par-bond approximation (sanity check: 2008
$+21$\%, 2022 $-16$\%), LBMA gold and Treasury bill returns. These are research
constructs and never investable sleeves. The classifier labels months from 1960
(\quita{789} \nuevo{790} months, 2.4 times the modern window, containing the actual 1970s
stagflation). Finally, a \emph{virgin confirmatory universe}: nine Ken French
international sleeves (Europe, Japan and Asia-Pacific ex-Japan, crossed with
market, value and momentum), USD, monthly, from November 1990 onward, never
downloaded or inspected during development, with the test protocol and thresholds
committed to the repository before the single run (Section 8).

\begin{nuevotexto}
\head{Factor data and descriptive statistics.} Strategies are priced against Ken French's
global factors: the developed-markets set (23 countries) for market, size, value,
profitability, investment and momentum, and the emerging-markets market factor, monthly in US
dollars from July 1990, with the one-month Treasury bill as the risk-free rate. Each factor is a
long-short portfolio, for instance value is cheap stocks minus expensive ones, so its return is
a premium rather than an investable fund. Exhibit~\ref{ex:desc} describes the 28 sleeves;
Appendix B describes the factors. Every sleeve fell by 41\% or more at its worst, and market betas
run from 0.72 to 1.27: however different the labels, these are all equity indices. The tilts do earn
something. Each region's factor sleeves beat its plain index by 1.67\% a year from 2009 (2.08\% from
2004) after charging the higher fee of a factor fund, $t = 2.3$ and $3.4$; in the live-index era from
2015, free of pre-launch back-filling, the figure is 1.96\% with $t = 1.9$.
\end{nuevotexto}

\section{Method}

\subsection{The regime layer and a pre-registered estimator}

Growth and inflation composites (z-scored, sign-adjusted trends of several
indicators each) define four quadrants: Goldilocks, Reflation, Deflationary bust
and Stagflation, with soft probabilities and an empirical monthly transition
matrix.\nuevo{ In plain terms, each month is labelled by whether growth and inflation are rising or
falling: rising growth with falling inflation is Goldilocks, rising both is Reflation, falling both
is a Deflationary bust, and falling growth with rising inflation is Stagflation. Months sharing a
label are treated as one group even when decades apart, so the 1970s and 2022 can inform each
other.} Two design facts matter downstream. The classifier is deterministic and
identical across eras, and its per-quadrant factor patterns are structural, with
15 of 16 factor-by-quadrant sign cells agreeing between 1960--2026 and the modern
window. The single flip is the market factor in stagflation.

\begin{nuevotexto}
\head{What shrinkage is.} An average computed from few observations mixes signal with luck. If an
index returned 0.47\% a month over 82 stagflation months, some of that is real and some is chance,
and nothing in those 82 months says how much of each. Shrinkage is the standard remedy: rather than
trusting the noisy estimate, move it part of the way toward a steadier reference value,
\[
\text{final estimate} = \text{weight} \times \text{noisy estimate} + (1-\text{weight}) \times
\text{steady reference}.
\]
This accepts a small bias in exchange for much less noise, and usually gains on balance. A
scout does the same with a striker who scored three goals a game over ten games, pulling the number
back toward what strikers typically score. This study uses two different shrinkages.
\citet{ledoit2004} shrinkage acts on the covariance matrix, how assets move together, and pulls it
toward a simple structure; minimum variance, equal risk contribution and hierarchical risk parity
all rely on it, and it is standard. The second is our own and acts on average returns. It is not a
Markowitz optimization: no contestant runs classic mean-variance on these means, and the covariance
is not split by regime. Its peculiarity is that it works regime by regime, borrowing evidence from
earlier decades that were in the same macroeconomic state.
\end{nuevotexto}

On top of it we build, freeze and pre-register a transparent estimator for the
noisiest objects in the exercise, the per-regime conditional means, at \quita{30 to 90} \nuevo{71 to 101 (as few as 14 at the first refit)}
monthly observations per cell. We state it because Section 7.2 reports that it has
no effect resolvable at this sample size, and the construction and its
null result are inseparable. Write $\hat{e}_{is}$ for the modern conditional excess of factor sleeve $i$ in state $s$:
the mean monthly return of $i$ across the training months labelled $s$, minus the mean of its
regional Reference sleeve across the same months. Each factor family maps to a long counterpart
$j$ among the Fama-French research factors, Enhanced Value to HML and Momentum to MOM, with
Quality having none and staying modern. Then $\bar{f}_{js}$ is that counterpart's mean return in
state $s$ over the 66-year sample and $\bar{f}^{\,\prime}_{js}$ is the same quantity over the
modern window alone. The two sample sizes are the months available in state $s$ on each side,
$n_s$ modern and $m_s$ long, and $m_s \gg n_s$ throughout: \quita{789} \nuevo{790} classifiable long months against
roughly 330 modern ones, which is why the anchor dominates wherever the gate opens. Finally
$\beta_j$ translates academic long-short factor units into long-only sleeve excess units,
estimated once per family as the ordinary-least-squares slope of the pooled modern sleeve excess
on $f_j$ over their overlap; measured values \quita{run from 0.19 to 0.28} \nuevo{are 0.21 for value and 0.26 for momentum}. With $\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}$
the indicator function, the estimator is a gate and a blend

\begin{equation}
g_{js} = \mathbf{1}\!\left\{ \operatorname{sign}(\bar{f}_{js})
       = \operatorname{sign}(\bar{f}^{\,\prime}_{js}) \right\}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\tilde{e}_{is} = g_{js} \cdot
  \frac{n_s \hat{e}_{is} + m_s \beta_j \bar{f}_{js}}{n_s + m_s}
  + (1 - g_{js})\, \hat{e}_{is}
\end{equation}

The gate asks one question of the long series: does its 66-year record in state $s$ agree in
sign with what that same series did in the modern era? If the two eras disagree about direction,
nothing transfers and the modern estimate stands. If they agree, the blend is a precision-weighted
average of the modern estimate and the $\beta$-mapped long one, weighted by the months of evidence
behind each. This is empirical-Bayes pooling\nuevo{ (letting a large, related sample inform a
small one)} with a pretest gate\nuevo{ (a preliminary check that decides whether to pool at
all)} on the crudest sufficient statistic, the sign. It feeds the
\citet{black1992} view vector and the worst-quadrant objective's per-regime means,
and reporting always shows raw modern means. Full treatment, including the
asset-class and no-counterpart cases, is in the repository.

\begin{nuevotexto}
Exhibit~\ref{ex:worked} works the rule through on real numbers. Take Enhanced Value in Stagflation.
Over 82 modern months it beat its regional index by 0.47\% a month. The academic value factor, over
180 stagflation months since 1960, translates into only 0.12\% a month in sleeve units. The two eras
agree on the direction, so the gate opens and the months of evidence set the weights: 69\% on the long
record, giving 0.23\%. The modern record looked twice too good, and the long record tempers it.
Where the eras disagree, as for Momentum in a Deflationary bust, the gate closes and the modern
figure stands. Quality has no long academic counterpart and always stays modern.
\end{nuevotexto}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\exhibittitle{\nuevo{The estimator on real numbers (percent per month, full sample)}}{ex:worked}
\fontsize{8}{9.6}\selectfont
{\color{nuevoc}\input{tables/tab_worked}}
\exhibitnote{\nuevo{Excess return of the factor sleeves over their regional index in each macro state.
$n$: modern months; $m$: months since 1960. Long, mapped: the academic factor's average in that

\begin{nuevotexto}
Three features of this construction limit how much it can claim. The long sample contains the modern
months, so those months are counted on both sides and the weight on the long record is overstated.
For the same reason the gate compares a sample with its own subset, so agreement is easier than
it looks. And the long record is the US, applied to regional indices.
\end{nuevotexto}

\subsection{Contestants, protocol and inference}

We field equal weight (1/N), minimum variance, equal risk contribution (ERC) and
hierarchical risk parity (HRP), all on \citet{ledoit2004} shrunk covariances\nuevo{ (the
sample covariance pulled toward a simple structured target, which tames estimation noise)}; a
mean-variance blend built around a Black-Litterman posterior;
cross-sectional momentum (12-1, top 6), unlevered volatility targeting
\citep{moreira2017}, binary trend overlays \citep{faber2007,antonacci2014},
worst-quadrant maximin, which maximizes the mean return in whichever of the four macro states turns out worst, both unconstrained and under diversified caps (per-sleeve at most 25\%, look-through geographic at most 40\%, factor at most 40\%), and an
all-weather diversified maximin on the menu extended with Treasury, gold and cash
proxies. We also field the three most-cited ``beat-1/N'' rules as contestants: the
\citet{yuan2023} global minimum-variance combination, the \citet{brodie2009}
sparse portfolio (in long-only form minimum variance at a target return, the
$\ell_1$ penalty being inert), and HERC in both linkages. Raw full-sample mean
returns are forbidden as objective inputs throughout.

The protocol is an expanding-window walk-forward with a 120-month warmup, annual
refits, every input re-estimated on training data only, and returns net of 10
basis points of one-way transaction costs on turnover.\nuevo{ In plain terms: each January a
rule sees only the months before it, chooses its weights, holds them for the next twelve
months, and is scored on those months, exactly as an investor would have lived them. Section 5.4
repeats the race with shorter warmups, which moves the start of scoring back to 2002, and with
rolling windows of 36 to 120 months, which test how much estimation length matters. Turnover is the
share of the portfolio traded at a refit; a basis point is one hundredth of one percent.} Companion races are a
90-year re-race on the proxy universe (out of sample 1936--2026) with
shifted-start variants, hand-dated episode replays, and a regime-persistent
stationary bootstrap used as forward validator and never as objective. Inference
is \citet{ledoit2008} heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent\nuevo{ (robust to
volatility that changes over time and to returns correlated from one month to the next)}
delta-method plus a studentized circular block bootstrap ($B = 4999$,
$b \approx T^{1/3}$, sensitivity $b \in \{3,6,10\}$) for every contestant against 1/N and against minimum variance as the incumbent winner, deflated Sharpe with the fielded-roster
trial count, and CSCV probability of backtest overfitting ($S = 16$, 12,870
half-splits). We use the bootstrap rather than the classical Sharpe test because
monthly Sharpe differences carry heavy tails and autocorrelation, which that test
assumes away.

\begin{quitado}
Sharpe ratios use a zero risk-free rate throughout, tables and text alike. On the
148 of 210 out-of-sample months for which a Treasury-bill series is available,
recomputing in excess terms on that same subset moves the headline $p$ from 0.180
to 0.209 and the Sharpe gap from $+0.163$ to $+0.151$, so the convention is not
load-bearing. What separates those figures from the 0.055 of the full sample is
the shorter window, not the choice of convention.
\end{quitado}

\begin{nuevotexto}
All ratios and alphas use returns in excess of the one-month Treasury bill. Version 1.0 reported
Sharpe ratios at a zero risk-free rate because the bill series appeared to cover only 148 of the
210 out-of-sample months. That gap was an alignment artefact, not missing data: the index levels
are stamped on the last business day of each month and the bill on the last calendar day, and a
join on exact dates keeps only the months where the two coincide. Matched by month, the bill
covers all 210, and the switch moves the headline $p$ from 0.055 to 0.065 and the Sharpe gap
from $+0.20$ to $+0.19$. No conclusion changes.

Section 5.3 adds further measures, each tested against 1/N. Sortino and Treynor differences use
a paired circular block bootstrap with the same block length, replications and seed as the
Sharpe test. Alphas are intercepts of regressions of a strategy's monthly excess return on the
monthly factor returns, with \citet{newey1987} standard errors at a lag of four months. The alpha
of a strategy \emph{relative to} 1/N is the intercept of the same regression run on the return
difference between the two, which equals the difference of their alphas. With this many
regressors the usual standard errors are too optimistic, so we report $p$-values from a studentized
bootstrap that resamples whole months of returns and factors together, and Romano-Wolf adjusted
$p$-values, which allow for having tested many rules: an adjusted $p$ below 0.05 means the result would
be unusual even as the best of the whole family. The primary factor model was fixed in writing and
committed to the repository before it was run, after exploratory evidence had already pointed
toward its likely result, so it blocks further specification search but is not a blind test.

\head{Reading the statistics.} A $p$-value is the probability of seeing a gap at least as large
as the one observed if the two strategies were in truth equally good; below 0.05 we call a
difference significant. Power is the reverse question: the probability that the test would
detect a gap of a given size if it were real, and it is only meaningful for a gap chosen in advance,
because power at the observed gap merely restates the $p$-value \citep{hoenig2001}. A test with low
power can miss a real difference, so a non-significant result means ``not shown'', never ``equal''.
Each ratio is annualized, and a Sharpe ratio of 0.75 means 0.75 percentage points of return above
Treasury bills for each point of volatility. The bootstrap estimates these
probabilities by resampling the data instead of assuming that returns are normally distributed,
which monthly returns are not.
\end{nuevotexto}

Exhibit~\ref{ex:race} has one headline. Minimum variance tops it, and its edge over 1/N is
not significant.

The rest of the table says the same thing in different ways. No contestant clears 5\% against
equal weight: minimum variance reaches a bootstrap $p$ of \quita{0.055} \nuevo{0.065} and every other rule sits at
$p \ge \quita{0.14}\nuevo{0.17}$. \quita{What the data can detect is the downside. Equal weight plus volatility targeting
is significantly worse than plain 1/N, and dual momentum worse still.} \nuevo{Nor is any rule
significantly worse: 1/N with volatility targeting and dual momentum sit at $p = 0.07$ and $0.08$.
A reader may object that ``beats'' calls for a one-sided test, and one-sided the minimum-variance
gap reaches $p = 0.025$. But that is the best of sixteen rules, and the Romano-Wolf adjustment for
having tried sixteen puts it at $p = 0.47$. Moreover a reader may object to the benchmark, since 1/N
over nested indices is not quite naive; on the 19 non-overlapping sleeves the result is the same
(0.95 against 0.73, $p = 0.064$).}

The verdict survives a joint test as well as the pairwise ones. A Friedman test on 12-month
block ranks\nuevo{, which asks whether the ranking as a whole is better than chance,} rejects the null that the ordering is noise ($\chi^{2} = \quita{46.6}\nuevo{30.7}$\nuevo{, $p = 0.015$}), yet the Nemenyi
critical difference\nuevo{, the smallest rank gap that counts once all pairs are compared at
once,} clears no contestant past 1/N. The ranking is real; the gap to equal weight
is not. Multiplicity does not rescue anything either: deflated Sharpe ratios of 0.98 and above
clear that bar, and the probability that the in-sample-selected contestant is no better than
the out-of-sample median is \quita{33\%} \nuevo{36\%}, which is real selection information well short of
certainty.

\head{What that non-rejection is worth.} A $p$ above 0.05 licenses ``no effect''
only if the design could have found one, so we report the power of our own
headline test, meaning the chance it would have flagged an edge of that size as
significant had one really existed, computed on the same standard error the test
uses. \quita{Against the largest gap
in Exhibit~\ref{ex:race}, minimum variance's $+0.20$ annualized Sharpe, the design
has 56\% power at the 5\% level.} \nuevo{The design would detect a true
gap of $+0.10$ annualized Sharpe 18\% of the time, $+0.20$ 56\% of the time and $+0.30$ 88\% of the
time. Those gaps are fixed in advance; power computed at the observed gap would merely restate the
$p$-value.} The smallest gap the design could detect at a given target power, its minimum detectable effect size, follows from the same standard error. Writing $\pi$ for that target and $\alpha$ for the significance level,

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{MDES} \;=\; \left(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{\pi}\right) \mathrm{se},
\end{equation}

\noindent where $z$ denotes a standard normal quantile. At $\alpha = 0.05$ and $\pi = 0.80$ the
bracket is 2.80, so the minimum detectable gap is 2.80 standard errors, or $+0.27$
annualized Sharpe here. Because $\mathrm{se}$ falls with $\sqrt{T}$, that
threshold is a property of the sample length before it is a property of any estimator. The observed gap is \quita{three quarters} \nuevo{seven tenths} of the
detectable one. The correct statement is therefore weaker than the literature's
usual phrasing, and we adopt it throughout: no rule beats 1/N resolvably at this sample size. Whether a \quita{$+0.20$} \nuevo{$+0.19$} edge exists is a question 210 monthly
observations cannot answer either way. \quita{Section 6 matters because the menu
measurement is not subject to the same limit.}

Two further facts constrain how far the modern race travels, and they point the
same way. The winner's return is 82\% attributable to Quality sleeves (below),
and Quality is the defensive factor a post-2009 window rewards. In the 90-year
proxy race of Section 5.2 the same rule falls to last among structural rules\quita{ and
beats 1/N in only 25\% of shifted-start windows}\nuevo{, though only as a point estimate (0.50 against
0.56, $p = 0.21$)}. The most economical reading of
the two together is that minimum variance's modern lead is a regime-shaped factor
bet and not a durable property of the method.

None of the three most-cited rules designed to beat 1/N does so on this menu. The

their own theory predicts where the estimation window is short and the menu
one-factor-dominated, and we declared the prediction before running.
\citeauthor{brodie2009}'s \citeyearpar{brodie2009} sparse portfolio reaches \quita{third
place (0.93) at only $p = 0.149$} \nuevo{third place (0.84) at only $p = 0.193$}, so their ``significantly and consistently'' does
not survive the Sharpe-difference test and the transaction charge they never
applied. HERC lands below both its parents.

Two mechanical facts explain why nothing separates. The contestants' out-of-sample
returns are \quita{0.93 to 0.998} \nuevo{0.78 to 0.999} correlated with one another\nuevo{, among the twelve equity rules without
overlays}. Hierarchical risk parity
and equal risk contribution at 0.998 are one portfolio under two names, and
Brodie and minimum variance at 0.975 earn from the same USA Quality sleeve, so
the seventeen-row table is roughly four distinct strategies, and no Sharpe test
can pull apart series that move together this closely. Attribution then shows
what the winner actually is. Minimum variance earns 82\% of its out-of-sample return in Quality sleeves (USA 52\%, World 30\%), which is the
low-volatility-anomaly mechanism made visible: a defensive factor bet carrying an
optimizer's name. \quita{Both facts point past the optimizer to the menu, which
Section 6 measures.}

$0.84$).}

\subsection{Long history and the constraint grids}

\begin{quitado}
Re-raced over 1936--2026 on six long-only Fama-French portfolios, minimum variance
falls to last among structural rules (0.71) while hierarchical risk parity (0.76)
and equal risk contribution (0.75) edge 1/N (0.74). Across shifted-start variants
both beat 1/N in 100\% of windows and minimum variance in 25\%. The
modern menu shows the same signature in rolling windows, with equal risk
contribution and hierarchical risk parity beating 1/N in 98 to 99\% of rolling
three-year windows. The structural rules hold their advantage across both eras; minimum variance does not.
\end{quitado}
\begin{nuevotexto}
Re-raced over 1936--2026 on six long-only Fama-French portfolios, in excess returns, the four rules
cannot be told apart: hierarchical risk parity 0.56 ($p = 0.53$ against 1/N), 1/N 0.56, equal risk
contribution 0.56 ($p = 0.46$) and minimum variance 0.50 ($p = 0.21$). Version 1.0's statement that
the structural rules hold an advantage over 1/N across both eras does not survive a test. Minimum
variance's modern lead is absent from the long record, but so is any demonstrated loss.
\end{nuevotexto}

\subsection{\nuevo{Beyond the Sharpe ratio: downside, beta, active risk and alpha}}

\begin{nuevotexto}
The contestants with the best Sharpe ratios in Exhibit~\ref{ex:race} tend to be the ones furthest
to the left of the risk-return plane, which invites the suspicion that the ranking rewards low
volatility rather than anything a rule does. The Sharpe ratio cannot be raised by leverage, so a
low-risk portfolio does not score higher by construction, but a low-risk portfolio can harvest
the low-volatility anomaly \citep{haugen1991,frazzini2014}, the long-documented tendency of calmer
stocks to earn more than their risk implies, and a single ratio cannot tell that apart from skill.
We therefore re-rank the race five ways. With $R$ a strategy's return, $R_f$ the Treasury bill,
$\bar{x}$ a time average and $\sigma(\cdot)$ a volatility,

\begin{align*}
\text{Sharpe} &= \frac{\overline{R-R_f}}{\sigma(R-R_f)}, &
\text{Sortino} &= \frac{\overline{R-R_f}}{\sigma_{\text{down}}(R-R_f)}, &
\text{Treynor} &= \frac{\overline{R-R_f}}{\beta}, \\[4pt]
\text{Information} &= \frac{\overline{R-R_{1/N}}}{\sigma(R-R_{1/N})}, &
\text{Appraisal} &= \frac{\alpha}{\sigma(\varepsilon)}, &
R-R_f &= \alpha + \textstyle\sum_k b_k F_k + \varepsilon,
\end{align*}

\noindent where $\sigma_{\text{down}}$ counts only the months below the bill, $\beta$ is the
sensitivity to the global market, the $F_k$ are the factor returns with loadings $b_k$, $\alpha$ is
the return the factors leave unexplained, and $\varepsilon$ the residual. Sortino asks whether the
avoided volatility was the harmful kind; Treynor charges only for market risk; alpha asks whether
anything is left once the strategy's exposures have been paid for; information and appraisal ratios
ask how steadily that happens.
\end{nuevotexto}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\exhibittitle{\nuevo{Four ways to adjust for risk, 2009--2026}}{ex:riskadj}
\fontsize{8}{9.6}\selectfont
{\color{nuevoc}\input{tables/tab_riskadj}}
\exhibitnote{\nuevo{210 out-of-sample months, excess returns, net of transaction costs. $\beta$
on the developed-markets market factor. Sortino and Treynor (annualized excess return per unit of
$\beta$) with the $p$-value of their difference against 1/N from a paired circular block
bootstrap. $\alpha$ in percent a year with its Newey-West $t$-statistic, against the CAPM (market
only) and the Carhart four-factor model (market, size, value, momentum). Sorted by Sharpe
ratio.}}
\end{table}

\begin{nuevotexto}
\head{Downside risk.} The Sortino ratio leaves the top of the ranking where it was. Minimum
variance leads at 1.49 against 1/N's 1.20 ($p = 0.17$). The only difference below 5\% is a
loss, 1/N with volatility targeting ($p = 0.03$).

\head{Market risk.} The Treynor ratio re-ranks in the direction the concern predicts: the highest
values belong to the all-weather maximin (17.7\%, beta 0.32) and the trend overlay (16.3\%, beta
0.46). That is the measure working as designed, not a better portfolio. Treynor assumes a portfolio
is one holding inside a diversified whole, so a portfolio that already holds other asset classes is
credited for diversification the ratio assumes it lacks. So it does not answer the concern; if
anything it sharpens it. Among equity-only rules minimum variance leads again (14.9\% against 11.9\%,
$p = 0.08$).

\head{Alpha.} Against the global market minimum variance earns a CAPM alpha of $+3.0$\% a year
($t = 2.7$), which is the low-volatility anomaly at work. Against 1/N the alpha is $+2.5$\% ($p = 0.08$), and
the Carhart model leaves it at $+2.4$\% ($p = 0.06$).

One specification looks like a discovery and is not. The gap between minimum variance and 1/N
contains a large regional bet, loading $+0.27$ on developed markets and $-0.40$ on emerging ones,
because 1/N keeps nearly a third of its capital in emerging and Asian sleeves and minimum variance
almost none. Adding an emerging-market factor removes those swings and the same $+2.4$\% looks highly
significant ($p = 0.004$). We chose that model after seeing the data. The full family of tests
gives it a Romano-Wolf $p$ of 0.27, and the alpha is the raw gap of $+1.2$\% plus a credit for the
gap's low beta. Netting out emerging markets without that credit leaves $+0.7$\% ($t = 0.6$).

So we fixed one primary model before computing it, built to price everything we know this gap
contains: the five regional markets of the menu, the size, value, profitability, investment and
momentum factors, and betting-against-beta, the academic measure of the low-risk premium. Under that
model the alpha of minimum variance over 1/N is $+0.24$\% a year (95\% interval $-1.4$ to $+1.8$,
$p = 0.76$), with no significant cell among the sixteen contestants (smallest adjusted $p = 0.46$). The
interval matters: effects below about 2.3\% a year could not have been detected, so this is no
detectable alpha, not zero alpha. The raw gap of $+1.23$\% decomposes into profitability
($+0.66$), low beta ($+0.51$), regional terms that nearly cancel ($+0.12$), momentum ($-0.38$), size
($+0.08$) and alpha ($+0.24$).
\end{nuevotexto}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\exhibittitle{\nuevo{Alpha over 1/N under five factor models, 2009--2026}}{ex:alpha}
\fontsize{8}{9.6}\selectfont
{\color{nuevoc}\input{tables/tab_alpha_vs_1n}}
\exhibitnote{\nuevo{Each cell is the alpha of the strategy relative to 1/N, in percent a year, with its
studentized-bootstrap $p$-value in parentheses; bold marks $p < 0.05$ before any adjustment for
multiple testing, and no cell survives that adjustment. CAPM: developed-markets factor. 4F adds size,
value and momentum; ``+ EM'' adds the emerging-markets factor; FF5 adds profitability (RMW) and
investment (CMA); P is the primary model described in the text.}}
\end{table}

\begin{nuevotexto}
Is the tilt skill? The data do not say. Minimum variance cannot be told apart from a naive
alternative chosen in advance, equal weight over the seven Quality sleeves (Sharpe 0.82, $p = 0.17$
against minimum variance), but neither can that alternative be told from 1/N ($p = 0.26$). It is
ahead of inverse-variance weighting at $p = 0.06$. Only the hindsight pair of USA and World Quality
matches it (0.96).

\head{Active risk.} The information ratio measures a strategy against 1/N directly: the average
return gap divided by the volatility of that gap, the tracking error. Minimum variance finished ahead
of 1/N in 97\%, 99\% and 100\% of rolling three-, five- and ten-year windows, yet its information ratio
of 0.22 is far from significant ($p = 0.43$): a gap of 1.2\% a year is small against a tracking error of
5.7\%. Overlapping windows are not independent, so those shares describe consistency and do not
test it. They also explain the non-significance better than any talk of redundancy: this is a real
departure from 1/N over too few years. The information ratio has a blind spot: it compares raw
returns, so a portfolio with less market exposure looks worse in a rising market. The all-weather
maximin has a Sharpe ratio above 1/N's and a significantly negative information ratio ($-0.52$,
$p = 0.03$). That is why it cannot be the only yardstick here, whatever its merits for managers
measured against a benchmark. The appraisal ratio avoids the blind spot by using alpha in place of the
raw gap, but it restates the alpha $t$-statistic per year and adds no independent evidence.
\end{nuevotexto}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\exhibittitle{\nuevo{Against the benchmark: information and appraisal ratios, 2009--2026}}{ex:active}
\fontsize{8}{9.6}\selectfont
{\color{nuevoc}\input{tables/tab_active}}
\exhibitnote{\nuevo{Active is the average annual return gap to 1/N and TE its volatility (the
tracking error); IR is their ratio, with the Newey-West $p$-value of the mean gap. Appraisal
ratio: alpha divided by residual volatility, for the strategy against the CAPM and the four-factor
model, and for the strategy's return gap to 1/N under the four-factor model plus the

strategy's cumulative return beat 1/N's (overlapping windows; descriptive, not a test).}}
\end{table}

\begin{nuevotexto}
\head{Risk aversion.} The certainty-equivalent return, the riskless return an investor would swap the
strategy for, answers the left-of-the-plane worry directly, because it depends on how much the
investor dislikes risk. At low risk aversion ($\gamma = 1$, the value in \citealp{demiguel2009})
no rule beats 1/N and the overlays lose, volatility targeting by 3.6\% a year ($p = 0.009$). At
$\gamma = 10$ the low-volatility rules gain, minimum variance by 3.8\% ($p = 0.014$) and hierarchical
risk parity by 1.0\% ($p = 0.013$). None survives adjustment for sixteen rules, and an investor
that averse would hold Treasury bills alongside, not a fully invested equity portfolio.

\head{Fees.} The race charges trading costs but, because it measures indices, no fund fee. Charging
illustrative ETF expense ratios on the weights each contestant held (0.15\% a year for plain market
indices, 0.30\% for factor indices, 0.10\% more for emerging and Asian lines) lowers every Sharpe ratio
by about 0.02 and changes no conclusion; minimum variance against 1/N moves from $p = 0.065$ to $0.070$
(Appendix B).
\end{nuevotexto}

\subsection{\nuevo{Longer and shorter windows: bringing the bear markets into the race}}

\begin{nuevotexto}
The 120-month warmup places the whole race inside one post-crisis expansion. Exhibit~\ref{ex:warmup}
re-runs it with warmups of 80 and 60 months, so that scoring starts in September 2005 and January
2004 and contains the 2007--09 bear market; a 36-month warmup reaches back to 2002. These windows
nest one another, so they are not independent votes. They also keep expanding, so from 2009 they use
exactly the same training data as the baseline and say nothing about estimation length. For that we
use rolling windows, which forget old data and are the design of \citet{demiguel2009}.
\end{nuevotexto}

\begin{table}[H]

\exhibittitle{\nuevo{The race on three warmups, and through the 2008 crisis}}{ex:warmup}
\fontsize{8}{9.6}\selectfont
{\color{nuevoc}\input{tables/tab_warmup}}
\exhibitnote{\nuevo{Excess-return Sharpe ratio and bootstrap $p$-value against 1/N for each warmup
(months of data before the first scored month). GFC return: cumulative total return from November

\end{table}

\begin{nuevotexto}
The verdict holds. Minimum variance is first with warmups of 120, 80 and 60 months and its margin
over 1/N stays at the threshold or above it ($p = 0.065$, $0.050$, $0.068$), weakening to $0.20$ from 2002.
Rolling windows of 120, 80, 60 and 36 months give minimum variance Sharpe ratios of 0.93, 0.91, 0.91 and
0.75 against 1/N's 0.75 ($p = 0.09$, $0.11$, $0.11$, $0.94$): a shorter memory costs little down to five
years and the entire edge at three. The unconstrained Yuan-Zhou combination is outside its own domain
at 36 months (28 assets per 36 observations) and collapses. A longer window lowers the minimum
detectable gap from 0.27 to 0.22, but the observed gap shrinks with it.

The bear markets change the overlays, and less than version 1.0 of this article implied. The trend and
volatility overlays are crisis insurance. From November 2007 to February 2009 the trend overlay lost
21\%, dual momentum 23\%, volatility targeting 39\%, minimum variance 45\% and 1/N 55\%. Over those
crisis months they earn their keep; outside them volatility targeting loses steadily: excluding
that episode it is worse than 1/N at $p = 0.04$, and over the live-index era at $p = 0.02$. One crash
cannot settle whether that insurance is worth its cost. Minimum variance is not universal protection
either. From January 2002 to March 2003 it lost 19\% against 1/N's 14\%, though it was then fitted
on only 36 months, the very setting that removes its edge. Over 2004--2008 it trailed 1/N (0.10 against
0.18), missing most of an emerging-market rally of about a third a year.
\end{nuevotexto}

\section{The opportunity set}

\begin{figure}[H]
\exhibittitle{The equity menu cannot reach below 13.3\% volatility; the extended menu reaches 0.6\%}{ex:frontier}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{F0b_frontier_cloud.pdf}
\exhibitnote{The long-only frontier of each menu, with the individual sleeves and the fielded
rules, on a shared scale. Panel A: on 28 equity sleeves the frontier is a short arc and every
rule piles into the same corner. Panel B: adding Treasuries, gold and cash moves the floor to
0.6\% and the frontier sweeps the whole plane. Both frontiers are computed on the full sample, one solution per target return under
long-only weights. They show the shape of each opportunity set, not an out-of-sample result.}
\end{figure}

\quita{Why does no weighting rule beat 1/N here, when the literature's optimization
defenders show that it can? Because on an investable long-only factor menu there
is almost nothing to optimize. We measure it three ways.} \nuevo{The obvious explanation for
Section 5 is that this menu leaves almost nothing to optimize. We first measure how redundant it is, and
then test whether redundancy is in fact the explanation.}

\nota{figura de la v1 con correlaciones desfasadas y un error en la nota (el $DR^2$ de una cartera solo-largos nunca baja de 1). La sustituye la tabla de la Exhibit siguiente.}
\begin{figure}[H]
\color{quitarc}
\exhibittitle{\quita{Factor tilts do not decorrelate, and the menu holds about one bet}}{ex:dispersion}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{F0_dispersion.pdf}
\exhibitnote{Grey is equity, teal is asset classes. Panel A: the most correlated cut of the menu is
same-region, different-factors (0.885); only the non-equity sleeves are genuinely different
bets (Treasuries $-0.115$, gold $-0.007$). Panel B: independent risk bets ($DR^{2}$), with the
95\% bootstrap interval of Section 6. Below 1.0 a menu holds a single bet.}
\end{figure}

\head{First, correlation structure.} The highest-correlated cut of the entire
menu is \emph{same region, different factors}. Value, momentum and quality within
one country co-move at 0.885, higher than the same factor across regions (0.786)
or pure market beta\nuevo{ (how much an index moves with its market as a whole)} across regions (0.821). Long-only factor tilts do not
decorrelate, because each index is roughly its parent market plus a small tilt,
and the market beta dominates. The three non-equity proxies are the only genuinely
different bets on the menu, with Treasuries correlating \quita{$-0.115$ with the 28
equity sleeves and gold $-0.007$} \nuevo{$-0.11$ and gold $+0.05$ with the equal-weighted equity sleeves}.

\head{Second, independent bets.} The Choueifaty-Coignard diversification ratio compares the
risk of the sleeves held separately with the risk of the portfolio that holds them,

\begin{equation}
DR(w) \;=\; \frac{\sum_i w_i \sigma_i}{\sqrt{w' \Sigma w}},
\end{equation}

\noindent with $\sigma_i$ the standalone volatility of sleeve $i$ and $\Sigma$ the shrunk
covariance. The numerator is what the portfolio's risk would be if the sleeves never offset each
other; the denominator is what it actually is. When correlations cancel nothing the two coincide
and $DR = 1$, which is why $DR^{2}$ reads as an effective number of independent risk bets: it is
1 for a single bet and $N$ for $N$ uncorrelated ones of equal risk. (Defined with $|w_i|$ in
general; every portfolio here is long-only, so $w \ge 0$.) That number is 1.31 for the
equal-weighted equity menu, with a 95\% confidence interval of 1.24 to 1.40. The menu
holds about one and a third independent bets, and that figure is tightly estimated.\nuevo{ A quick
check explains the number. With similar volatilities, the ratio at equal weights is about one over the
average correlation, here $1/0.756 = 1.32$. So $DR^2$ restates mean correlation in units that read as
bets. It also depends on the weights and not only on the menu: the same 28 sleeves reach 1.46 under
the weights that maximize it.}

We attach inference to it because a contribution reported as a bare point estimate would not be
held to the standard this article applies to every Sharpe comparison. The interval comes from
the block bootstrap of Section 4.2, with the covariance re-shrunk inside every replicate so
that what is measured is the variability of the whole estimate-then-summarize chain rather than
of a fixed covariance.

One objection has to be met before those numbers mean anything. The regional menu nests:
ACWI contains World, which contains the USA, Europe and Japan sleeves, and World ex-USA
contains Europe and Japan. A reader may reasonably ask whether the redundancy is an artefact of
holding the same stocks several times over. It is not. Restricting the calculation to the five
regions that do not overlap, USA, Europe, Japan, emerging markets and AC Asia ex-Japan, leaves
19 sleeves and a $DR^{2}$ of \textbf{1.37} (95\% interval 1.28 to 1.47), slightly higher than
the full menu's 1.31 rather than lower, and the within-region cross-factor correlation is
unchanged at 0.884. Dropping the nested aggregates does not rescue the menu.

Two comparisons put the number in context. The four-sleeve minimum-variance portfolio holds
1.28 independent bets, so the engine whose entire job is to exploit correlations to
cancel risk, holding a quarter as many sleeves, finds no more of them than naive diversification
does. And twenty-four extra equity sleeves buy 0.03 of a bet. The eigenvalues say the same thing: the first principal component alone explains
77\% of variance and the covariance matrix is near-singular.

\begin{quitado}
\head{Third, the contrast that identifies the mechanism.} Adding the three
asset-class proxies moves the menu's minimum pairwise correlation from 0.53 to
$-0.14$ and its diversification ratio to 1.43. Under the paired version of the
same bootstrap, where one set of resampled months drives both menus, the
difference is $+0.120$, with a 95\% interval of $+0.101$ to $+0.144$ and $p = 0.0002$. Three sleeves buy more independent-bet content than twenty-eight
equity sleeves did, and that gap is resolved with a confidence the weighting race
never reaches. At this data scale the menu effect is measurable and the method effect is not.
\end{quitado}
\nota{dos errores en lo quitado: (1) $+0{,}12$ de 3 activos NO es m\'as que $+0{,}31$ de 28 sleeves; (2) comparaba una diferencia de $DR^2$, casi mec\'anica, con una de Sharpe.}
\begin{nuevotexto}
\head{Third, what another asset class does.} Adding Treasuries, gold and cash to the 28 sleeves at
equal weights moves the ratio only from 1.31 to 1.43, because they then receive just 3/31 of the
capital (Exhibit~\ref{ex:dr2}). The right comparison is the other way round. One world index with a
Treasury holds 2.01 bets; with gold and cash as well, 2.78, more than twice the 28 sleeves, with four
holdings. And at the weights that maximize the ratio, the extended menu reaches 3.79 against 1.46.
\end{nuevotexto}

\subsection{The long-only wrapper}

The literature that motivates factor investing measures \emph{long-short}
portfolios, in which buying the favoured stocks and shorting their opposites
removes the market beta and leaves the premium. An investor who cannot short holds
the premium together with the parent market, and the beta dominates whatever the
tilt contributes. We measure the consequence three independent ways, and they
agree. \emph{(i) Across factors:} \citet{ilmanen2012} report near-zero correlation
across factor constituents, whereas on long-only sleeves the within-region
cross-factor correlation is 0.885, the highest cut of our menu.
\emph{(ii) The value/momentum hedge reverses sign.} \citet{asness2013} put the correlation between the two long-short
premia at approximately $-0.50$, which is the standard argument for
holding both. On our sleeves it is $-0.088$ once each is measured in
excess of its parent index, about a fifth of theirs, and $+0.820$ in the
space an investor actually holds. The direction survives in excess space, so the
economic mechanism is real. The magnitude does not, and in investable form the
sign flips: an investor buying value and momentum indices for their mutual hedge
is buying two versions of the same market exposure. Regional spread is wide and
worth reporting, with Europe ($-0.301$) and Japan ($-0.217$) approaching the
published figure while emerging markets ($+0.017$) and AC Asia ($+0.069$) are
indistinguishable from zero. \emph{(iii) The defensive factor:} Quality's excess
over junk is positive in drawdowns in long-short form, but long-only Quality
carries a beta of 0.91 and \emph{falls in 6 of 6 regions} during the
worst decile of market months, cushioning 0.91 percentage points
($-7.95$\% against the Reference's $-8.87$\%). A cushion of that size is
attenuation and cannot serve as a hedge.

Beta dominance is \quita{the mechanism the headline result rests on, and it is} why the
diversification the factor literature promises is largely unavailable in the form
a retail investor can buy.

\subsection{\quita{The reconciliation}\nuevo{Does the menu decide? A test on twelve menus}}

\begin{quitado}
Optimization beats 1/N exactly where there is dispersion to exploit, on the
industry and factor-portfolio datasets of its defenders, where idiosyncratic
volatility is high and the covariance is well conditioned, which is Gelmini and
Uberti's own explanation (Section 2). An investable factor menu is the opposite
regime, with one dominant bet, a near-singular covariance, and no dispersion for
any weighting scheme to convert into an edge. The disagreement in the literature
concerns the opportunity set, and the retail factor investor sits squarely in the
region where 1/N cannot be beaten.

For the investor this is a selection problem: \emph{widen the menu before refining the weights.} Three asset classes buy more independent-bet content than
twenty-eight equity sleeves, and no amount of estimator sophistication
substitutes.
\end{quitado}
\nota{esto es lo m\'as importante de la auditor\'ia. Era la tesis de la v1, y nunca se hab\'ia probado con m\'as de un men\'u. Probada, no se sostiene. Lo redacto como hallazgo; revisa si quieres otro enfoque.}

\begin{nuevotexto}
If redundancy were the reason nothing beats 1/N here, the same rules should gain on menus that are
less redundant. That is DeMiguel's own explanation, and it is testable. Exhibit~\ref{ex:menus} runs
minimum variance, equal risk contribution and hierarchical risk parity, on the protocol of Section
4.2, across twelve menus: our sleeves, several subsets, the Ken French industry and size-value
portfolios, and the international sleeves. The menus range from 1.19 to 2.78 independent bets.
\end{nuevotexto}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\exhibittitle{\nuevo{The same rules on menus of very different dispersion}}{ex:menus}
\fontsize{7.5}{9}\selectfont
{\color{nuevoc}\input{tables/tab_menus}}
\exhibitnote{\nuevo{$N$ holdings, $\bar\rho$ mean pairwise correlation, $DR^2$ at equal weights and at its
maximum. 1/N: excess-return Sharpe ratio. Rule columns: Sharpe gap to 1/N, with bootstrap $p$ in parentheses;
bold marks $p < 0.05$ with no adjustment for multiple testing. Long-only, expanding Ledoit-Wolf covariance,
120-month warmup, annual refit, 10 basis points. Scoring starts ten years after the date shown.}}
\end{table}

\begin{nuevotexto}
The explanation fails. From 1999, the minimum-variance edge is \emph{largest} on the most redundant menus:
$+0.17$ to $+0.25$ on the size-value portfolios ($p = 0.03$ to $0.04$, before adjustment), against $+0.04$ to
$+0.08$ on the far more dispersed industries ($p > 0.5$). The rank correlation between the edge and $DR^2$ is
$-0.69$ ($p = 0.014$), the wrong sign. Since 1963 the sign is right ($+0.89$, on six overlapping menus) but
the effect has no economic size: every edge lies between $-0.03$ and $+0.05$, and none is near
significance. Equal risk contribution and hierarchical risk parity stay within 0.08 of 1/N on every equity
menu, significant only on the size-value portfolios, where the gaps are tiny (0.02 and under 0.08). Two readings fit. Minimum variance's edge is a feature of the post-2009 era, visible across
equity menus and absent over six decades. And these long-only rules rarely separate from 1/N on any menu,
dispersed or not.

We do not claim to refute the optimization side. Its evidence often rests on engines we do not field, with
short sales and estimated means, and those levers are fixed here at the position of a long-only investor.
The reconciliation may be right for them. What this test rules out is the shortcut that the retail
investor's menu is, by itself, why 1/N is hard to beat.

Changing the menu is another matter, and it needs the same yardstick. Version 1.0 compared a gap in $DR^2$
with a gap in Sharpe ratio, two different quantities, and the former is close to mechanical.
Exhibit~\ref{ex:widen} compares Sharpe ratios on both sides. Over 2009--2026 equal weight over a world index,
Treasuries and gold has a Sharpe ratio of 0.96 against 0.75 for the 28 sleeves, with half the volatility and a
drawdown of 16\% against 27\%; the gain in Sharpe ratio is large but unresolved ($p = 0.35$), because the two
portfolios differ so much that 210 months cannot separate them. Over 1972--2026, on long-history proxies,
it is resolved: adding Treasuries and gold raises the Sharpe ratio by 0.07 at equal weights ($p = 0.02$) and by
0.19 under equal risk contribution ($p = 0.03$), with drawdowns of 40\% and 22\% against 54\%. Those are
frictionless US constructs, tested without an adjustment for the several comparisons shown. The practical
statement survives, with a firmer footing than before and a narrower claim: to reduce risk, change what you
hold, because that works at once; expect a better risk-adjusted return from it only over decades.
\end{nuevotexto}
